title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
For Illinois, I’ve chosen to examine median home value (variable B25077_001). Housing markets vary dramatically across the state, from Chicago’s urban core to rural farming counties, but ACS estimates in sparsely populated areas often come with wider margins of error. I want to assess not only where property values are highest, but also which counties’ estimates are statistically reliable enough to inform housing policy or investment decisions.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:

my_state <- "IL"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25077_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                       estimate   moe moe_pct

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    21
2 Low confidence     27
3 Moderate           54


Based on the summary statistics, since the median is 5.27% and the 3rd quartile is 7.09%, the original 3%/6% thresholds would put most counties in “Moderate” or “Low”. As a result, 21 counties are classified as “High confidence”, 54 as “Moderate” and 27 as “Low confidence”.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM  popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 17001 Adams County, Illinois     155900   4554 65166    NA
2 17003 Alexander County, Illinois  58700  10578  5042    NA
3 17005 Bond County, Illinois      133100  13683 16627    NA
4 17007 Boone County, Illinois     198600   8350 53316    NA
5 17009 Brown County, Illinois     142200  19435  6320    NA
6 17011 Bureau County, Illinois    121900   3733 33027    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         21        514207.
2 Low confidence          27         11301.
3 Moderate                54         29429.


High confidence counties have an average population 45 times larger than Low confidence counties (514,207 vs 11,301), confirming that smaller counties yield less reliable ACS estimates. While 53% of counties are moderately reliable, the 27 Low confidence counties—all sparsely populated—would be risky to use for targeted policy decisions without additional data collection.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
What: The communities we know the least about in Illinois are its smallest, most rural counties. From my analysis, the 27 Low confidence counties—which include sparsely populated areas like Hardin, Pope, Calhoun, and Gallatin counties—have an average population of just 11,301 residents. These are precisely the places where ACS estimates are most unreliable, yet they represent a significant portion of Illinois’s geographic area.
Why: The survey is sample‑based, not a census, and reliability depends heavily on sample size. Smaller counties contribute fewer respondents, which produces wider margins of error around every estimate. The ACS’s own design prioritizes precision for larger populations, leaving rural communities with statistically noisy data.
Who: If a state agency distributing housing grants based on median home values, treating every county’s estimate as equally certain. Using the 27 Low confidence counties’ numbers at face value could misdirect funds—a county with an artificially high estimate might receive less aid than it actually needs, while another with a low estimate might be overlooked despite hidden poverty. The rural poor, already underserved, would be the ones hurt most.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenge: one function, five states
text:
Optional challenge: one function, five states
The county-level pull earlier in this report is hard-coded to one state. I wrapped it in a function, pull_county_reliability(), that takes a state abbreviation (plus optional variable and year) and returns each county’s estimate, margin of error, population, and moe_pct:

pull_county_reliability <- function(state_abbr, variable = "B25077_001", year = 2023) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(myvar = variable, pop = "B01003_001"),
    state = state_abbr,
    year = year,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    transmute(
      state = state_abbr,
      GEOID,
      NAME,
      estimate = myvarE,
      moe = myvarM,
      popE,
      moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100
    )
}

With purrr::map_dfr() the same analysis runs across several states at once. I picked five with very different settlement geographies: Illinois, Ohio, Georgia, Montana, and Wyoming — 428 counties in total.

states <- c("IL", "OH", "GA", "MT", "WY")

multi_state <- map_dfr(states, pull_county_reliability)

multi_state %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  )) %>%
  group_by(state, reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 15 × 4
   state reliability     n_counties avg_population
   <chr> <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
 1 GA    High confidence         22        302228.
 2 GA    Low confidence          93         16234.
 3 GA    Moderate                44         60540.
 4 IL    High confidence         21        514207.
 5 IL    Low confidence          27         11301.
 6 IL    Moderate                54         29429.
 7 MT    High confidence          6        112466.
 8 MT    Low confidence          40          6267.
 9 MT    Moderate                10         17959.
10 OH    High confidence         30        302595.
11 OH    Low confidence          10         26528.
12 OH    Moderate                48         50769.
13 WY    High confidence          2         73840.
14 WY    Low confidence           6          9072.
15 WY    Moderate                15         25177.


To measure the small-places-are-noisier pattern directly, I correlated county population (log scale) with moe_pct within each state:

multi_state %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(correlation = cor(log(popE), moe_pct))

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  state correlation
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 GA         -0.652
2 IL         -0.677
3 MT         -0.637
4 OH         -0.669
5 WY         -0.656



ggplot(multi_state, aes(popE, moe_pct, color = state)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 7, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Smaller counties, wider margins of error — in every state",
    x = "County population (log scale)",
    y = "Margin of error as % of estimate",
    color = "State"
  )








What I found: the small-places-are-noisier pattern holds everywhere. In all five states the correlation between population and moe_pct falls in a narrow band between -0.64 and -0.68, and the average High-confidence county is anywhere from 8× (Wyoming) to 45× (Illinois) more populous than the average Low-confidence county.
What differs between states is how much of the state is affected. In Montana, 40 of 56 counties and in Georgia, 93 of 159 fall into Low confidence, while in Ohio only 10 of 88 do. The rule is universal, but its footprint depends on settlement geography: states dominated by small rural counties simply have less trustworthy home-value data overall than states of evenly mid-sized counties like Ohio.

title: assignment-3
section: 3. Compute poverty rate and MOE for 2006–2010
text:
3. Compute poverty rate and MOE for 2006–2010
Compute the poverty rate and its margin of error for 2006–2010. If totalE is missing or zero, set the rate and MOE to NA instead of producing invalid values.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE,
      totalE,
      below_povertyM,
      totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

title: assignment-3
section: 8. Calculate the change and test significance
text:
8. Calculate the change and test significance
Calculate the change in poverty rate, the standard error of the difference, the difference MOE, the z-score, and whether the change is statistically detectable at the 90% confidence level.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 -
               poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

title: assignment-3
section: 9. Calculate coefficient of variation and reliability
text:
9. Calculate coefficient of variation and reliability
Calculate the coefficient of variation for each period and classify each estimate as reliable, somewhat reliable, or unreliable.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_tested %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = 
      case_when(
        cv_2006_2010 < 12 ~ "reliable",
        cv_2006_2010 <= 40 ~ "somewhat reliable",
        TRUE ~ "unreliable"
      ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = 
      case_when(
        cv_2013_2017 < 12 ~ "reliable",
        cv_2013_2017 <= 40 ~ "somewhat reliable",
        TRUE ~ "unreliable"
      )
  )

  poverty_plot,
  aes(x = tract_order, y = change_pp)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp,
      ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp
    ),
    width = 0
  ) +
  geom_point() +

3. Calculate the change and CV
Calculate the change in poverty rate, the standard error of the difference, the difference MOE, the z-score, and whether the change is statistically detectable at the 90% confidence level. Calculate the coefficient of variation for each period and classify each estimate as reliable, somewhat reliable, or unreliable.

  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 -

    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
I am using Option A, the provided article:

Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018. https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/

The article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several checkable claims, among them:

Citywide poverty stood at 26 percent.
Fairhill had a 61 percent poverty rate and the city’s lowest median income.
Eastwick had the largest jump of any neighborhood, from 12 to 26 percent poverty.
Holmesburg (majority white) rose from 2 to 19 percent; Mayfair rose from 1 to 14 percent.
Poverty rose in 22 majority-white neighborhoods.
The framing: a city “still not recovered,” with rising poverty and inequality.

Two cautions before any math. First, census tracts are not neighborhoods: the article aggregated tracts into neighborhood boundaries of its own choosing and never published which tracts went where, so my tract-level numbers will not exactly match theirs. Second, everything below treats the ACS as what it is — a sample — so every number carries a margin of error, and a claim is only as good as its error bars.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
section: Part 1 — Reconstruct the data behind the claim
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct the data behind the claim
Variables. I use table B17001 (ratio of income to poverty in the past 12 months), specifically:

B17001_002 — population with income below the poverty level,
B17001_001 — total population for whom poverty status is determined (the denominator).

The article’s claims are about poverty rates, so a numerator/denominator pair is required; a rate needs both, and the margin of error of a rate must be propagated from both (via moe_prop()), not borrowed from the count.
Survey and years. I pull survey = "acs5" for year = 2010 (the 2006–2010 window) and year = 2017 (the 2013–2017 window), matching the two periods the article names. The 5-year ACS is the only choice here: tract-level estimates do not exist in the 1-year ACS, and the article itself says it used the five-year figures.
Assumptions the article forces on me. It does not publish its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, so I work at the tract level for Philadelphia County (state 42, county 101; the city and county share boundaries), matching tracts across periods by GEOID. I define the poverty rate as below-poverty population divided by population with poverty status determined. I do not analyze the median-income or race-specific claims (they rest on other tables), and I set any tract with a zero or missing denominator to NA rather than letting it produce an invalid rate.
Do the two periods overlap? No. 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 share no calendar years, so the two samples are independent. That matters: the standard formula for the margin of error of a difference, \(\sqrt{MOE_1^2 + MOE_2^2}\), is exactly right for independent estimates. Had the windows overlapped (e.g., 2011–2015 vs. 2013–2017), the two estimates would share sample years, be positively correlated, and this formula would overstate the true margin of error of the change.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  below_poverty = "B17001_002",
  total         = "B17001_001"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
section: Part 2 — Test the change, tract by tract
text:
Part 2 — Test the change, tract by tract
For each tract and period I compute the poverty rate and its margin of error with moe_prop() — a rate is a proportion, and the count’s MOE does not carry over. If the denominator (totalE) is zero or missing, the rate is set to NA rather than allowed to produce nonsense.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_2017 <- acs_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013_2017",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


Next, the test statistics. The change is the difference of the two rates; its margin of error comes from combining the two standard errors (each \(SE = MOE / 1.645\), since ACS MOEs are at the 90 percent confidence level). The change counts as statistically detectable if \(|z| = |\text{change}/SE_{diff}| > 1.645\), the critical value for 90 percent confidence. I also compute each estimate’s coefficient of variation (\(CV = SE / \text{estimate} \times 100\)) and flag reliability with the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: \(CV < 12\) reliable, 12–40 somewhat reliable, \(> 40\) unreliable. Tracts whose rate is NA get NA reliability, not a fake label.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    )
  )



Missing values, investigated before decided on
Eight tracts produce NA rates. Before dropping anything, I look at why by pulling their raw denominators:


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(is.na(change)) %>%
  left_join(
    acs_2010 %>% select(GEOID, total_2010 = totalE),
    by = "GEOID"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    acs_2017 %>% select(GEOID, total_2017 = totalE),
    by = "GEOID"
  ) %>%
  select(NAME, total_2010, total_2017)

All eight are the classic “areas of no population” the ACS produces: Tract 50 plus the special-use 9800-series tracts (9803–9809), which in Philadelphia cover institutional and non-residential land such as the airport and parkland. Their population with poverty status determined is literally zero in both periods, so a poverty rate is undefined, not merely noisy. My decision: exclude these eight from the significance tests and every figure below, and say so — 384 − 8 = 376 testable tracts.


How much change is actually detectable?


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  summarise(
    total_tracts   = n(),
    excluded_na    = sum(is.na(significant)),
    detectable     = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detectable = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    detectable_up  = sum(significant & change > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    detectable_down = sum(significant & change < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

Show code

  filter(!is.na(change), !is.na(moe_diff), se_diff > 0)

poverty_complete %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rate_2006_2010 = mean(poverty_rate_2006_2010) * 100,
    avg_rate_2013_2017 = mean(poverty_rate_2013_2017) * 100,
    median_change_pp   = median(change) * 100,

1               25.5               26.1             1.15                     22


The headline numbers: of 376 testable tracts, only 63 (17 percent) show a change distinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence — 36 increases and 27 decreases. The remaining 313 tracts (83 percent) could plausively have not changed at all. The average tract poverty rate did drift up, from 25.5 to 26.1 percent, which squares with the article’s citywide “26 percent,” and 22 tracts still have poverty rates above 55 percent — concentrated poverty of the kind the article describes in Fairhill is real. But a city where five tracts out of six show no detectable change is not a city of surging poverty; it is a mostly flat city with real pockets of deepening distress.
One artifact deserves a flag: the single largest decrease belongs to special-use Tract 9800 (roughly 84 → 5 percent), an institutional tract whose population is group-quarters; its swing reflects who was housed there, not neighborhood change. The special-use series also wrecks precision: tracts 9891 and 9801 — group-quarters with a handful of residents — carry MOEs of ±221 and ±163 percentage points on their changes. Both survive the zero-denominator filter and both are (unsurprisingly) classified as not detectable, but their error bars are taller than the entire meaningful range of the chart, so Figure 1 clips its axis and says so.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Required evidence

Figure 1 — every tract’s change, with its margin of error
Each point is one of the 376 testable tracts, ordered from largest estimated decrease to largest estimated increase; the whiskers span the 90 percent margin of error of the change, and the dashed line marks zero. A tract counts as detectable only when its whiskers do not cross zero.


Show code
poverty_complete %>%
  mutate(
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_pp    = moe_diff * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(change_pp) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = change_pp, color = significant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_pp, ymax = change_pp + moe_pp),
    fatten = 0.5, linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#0072B2", "FALSE" = "grey60"),
    labels = c("Not detectable", "Detectable at 90% conf.")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-60, 70)) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Philadelphia tracts show no statistically detectable poverty change",
    subtitle = "376 census tracts, ordered by estimated change; whiskers are 90% MOE of the change.\nAxis clipped at -60/+70 points: two special-use tracts (9891, 9801) have error bars beyond ±160 points.",
    x = "Census tracts, ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-year estimates (2006–2010, 2013–2017) via tidycensus."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()





Change in tract poverty rate, 2006–2010 to 2013–2017, with 90% margins of error. A change is statistically detectable only where the error bar excludes zero.




The picture is blunt: for the grey majority, the error bar swallows the estimate. Some tracts’ changes are measured so imprecisely that the MOE is more than a hundred times the estimated change (e.g., Tract 306: −0.03 points, ±8.3). Only the blue points — where the whisker clears zero — support a claim that anything happened.


Table 1 — reliability of the tracts that moved the most
The table below lists the 15 largest statistically detectable increases, with each period’s CV color-coded by the Jurjevich thresholds (see the source note). This is exactly the population of tracts an article like this one quotes from — and even here, almost every 2006–2010 baseline is only “somewhat reliable” or worse.

  filter(!is.na(significant), significant, change > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(change)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  transmute(
    tract          = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    rate_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    rate_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    change_pp      = change * 100,
    moe_pp         = moe_diff * 100,

    cv_2013_2017

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate the article’s claims
Supported. The citywide level checks out: my average tract rate for 2013–2017 is 26.1 percent, matching the article’s “26 percent,” up from 25.5 in 2006–2010. Concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty is genuinely present — 22 tracts exceed 55 percent, several in the mid-60s. And the direction of the citywide story is right: among tracts with detectable change, increases (36) outnumber decreases (27), and the median change is +1.2 points. A city that was slightly poorer in 2013–2017 than in 2006–2010 is a fair summary.
Not supported. The sweeping framing — “startling” surges in poverty across neighborhoods — overstates what five-year tract data can show. 313 of 376 tracts (83 percent) show changes statistically indistinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence. Apparent jumps from very low baselines, exactly the Holmesburg (2%) and Mayfair (1%) pattern, are the least trustworthy numbers in the ACS: 44 tracts had unreliable 2006–2010 estimates (CV > 40), and a poverty rate of 1–2 percent is typically measured with an error band several times its size. Quoting “1 to 14 percent” without a margin of error is quoting noise-prone endpoints.
Cannot be determined. Every named-neighborhood figure — Fairhill 61%, Eastwick 12→26%, Holmesburg 2→19%, Mayfair 1→14%, Tioga-Nicetown’s income drop, Graduate Hospital’s $91,445 — would require the article’s tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, which it did not publish; my analysis deliberately stops at the tract level. The “22 majority-white neighborhoods” claim additionally needs poverty by race and a definition of majority-white. The white-poverty jump (14.8 → 19.4 percent) comes from a one-year survey, a different data product than the five-year comparison; and the citywide income figures rest on median-income tables (B19013-type) I did not test here.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 4: Rewrite the central paragraph
New five-year Census estimates paint a sobering but more nuanced picture of Philadelphia. Averaged across the city’s 384 census tracts, the poverty rate in 2013–2017 was about 26 percent, up modestly from 2006–2010. The average hides extremes: in more than 20 tracts, poverty exceeds 55 percent — echoing the deprivation reported in Fairhill — and eight tracts saw statistically confirmed increases of 20 percentage points or more. Yet most of the city did not measurably move: in 313 of 376 testable tracts, the change was too small to distinguish from sampling error. Because the American Community Survey is a sample, small-area figures carry wide margins of error — especially where poverty is rare — so dramatic neighborhood-level jumps deserve skepticism before they are believed.

Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

text:
Key Concepts
This lab introduced spatial data analysis in R using sf. Key concepts included coordinate reference systems (CRS), spatial joins, distance calculations, buffers, spatial filtering, and spatial intersections. I learned that st_transform() converts coordinates between CRSs, while st_join() matches observations based on location. We also used st_nearest_feature() and st_distance() to measure distance, and st_buffer() to create station service areas. Finally, we combined spatial operations with regular dplyr joins to identify low-income census tracts without access to Indego stations.

text:
Reflection
This lab helped me understand how spatial analysis can answer a practical policy question rather than simply produce a map. I found the distinction between joining by an attribute such as GEOID and joining by geographic location especially useful. The different definitions of access also showed me that spatial results depend strongly on methodological choices. For example, using a tract centroid, whether a tract touches a station buffer, or the percentage of tract area covered can produce different conclusions. I also learned that checking CRS, row counts, and missing values is important for avoiding misleading results.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
The article
I am using Option A, the provided article: Alfred Lubrano, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”, WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018.
It compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims:

Citywide poverty stood at 26 percent.
Fairhill had a 61 percent poverty rate.
Eastwick jumped from 12 to 26 percent, the largest rise of any neighborhood.
Holmesburg rose from 2 to 19 percent; Mayfair from 1 to 14 percent.
Poverty rose in 22 majority-white neighborhoods.

Census tracts are not neighborhoods, and the article never published which tracts went into which neighborhood, so I work at the tract level for Philadelphia County. My numbers will not match the article’s exactly — that is expected, not a failure.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct the data
I pull table B17001 at the tract level: B17001_002 (population below the poverty level) over B17001_001 (population for whom poverty status is determined). A poverty rate needs a numerator and a denominator, and its margin of error has to be propagated from both with moe_prop() — it does not carry over from the count. I use survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 (the 2006–2010 window) and year = 2017 (2013–2017), the two periods the article names, because tract-level estimates only exist in the 5-year ACS and the article says it used the five-year figures.
The article forces a few assumptions on me: it publishes no tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, so tract level is as far as I can go; Philadelphia County (state 42, county 101) matches the city boundary; tracts are matched across periods by GEOID; and any tract with a zero or missing denominator gets NA instead of an invalid rate. The two windows share no calendar years, so the two estimates are independent, and the standard MOE for a difference — sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²) — is exactly right here. If the windows overlapped, the estimates would be positively correlated and that formula would overstate the MOE of the change.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  below_poverty = "B17001_002",
  total         = "B17001_001"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 2: Test the change
For each tract and period I compute the poverty rate and its MOE with moe_prop(), setting the rate to NA wherever the denominator is zero or missing.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_2017 <- acs_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013_2017",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


Each ACS MOE is at 90 percent confidence, so the standard error is MOE / 1.645. The change is the difference of the two rates, its MOE is sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²), and the change counts as statistically detectable when the z-score clears the 90 percent critical value of 1.645. I also compute each estimate’s coefficient of variation (SE / estimate × 100) and flag reliability with the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12 reliable, 12–40 somewhat reliable, > 40 unreliable.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    )
  )


Eight tracts come back NA. Before deciding what to do with them, I checked why.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(is.na(change)) %>%
  left_join(acs_2010 %>% select(GEOID, total_2010 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  left_join(acs_2017 %>% select(GEOID, total_2017 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  select(NAME, total_2010, total_2017)

Their population with poverty status determined is zero in both periods, so a poverty rate is undefined, not merely noisy. I exclude them and test the remaining 376.

  summarise(

    excluded_na     = sum(is.na(significant)),

  summarise(

    avg_rate_2013_2017 = mean(poverty_rate_2013_2017) * 100,

Of 376 testable tracts, only 63 (17 percent) show a change distinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence — 36 up, 27 down. The other 313 (83 percent) could easily not have changed at all.
The average tract poverty rate did drift up, from 25.5 to 26.1 percent — which squares with the article’s citywide “26 percent” — and 22 tracts still sit above 55 percent, so the concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty the article describes is real. But a city where five tracts in six show no detectable change is mostly flat, not surging. One artifact needs a flag: the largest single “decrease” is special-use Tract 9800 (about 84 → 5 percent, group-quarters population), and special-use tracts 9891 and 9801 carry MOEs of ±221 and ±163 points, so the error-bar plot below clips its axis.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
The evidence
First, the required error-bar view: every tract’s change with its 90 percent MOE, ordered from largest decrease to largest increase, with zero marked. A tract only counts as changed when its whiskers clear zero.


Show code
poverty_complete %>%
  mutate(
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_pp    = moe_diff * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(change_pp) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = change_pp, color = significant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_pp, ymax = change_pp + moe_pp),
    fatten = 0.5
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-60, 70)) +
  scale_color_discrete(
    labels = c("Not detectable", "Detectable at 90% conf.")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Philadelphia tracts show no detectable poverty change",
    subtitle = "376 tracts ordered by estimated change; whiskers are 90% MOE of the change.
                Axis clipped at -60/+70 points (two special-use tracts' MOEs exceed +/-160).",
    x = "Census tracts, ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    color = NULL
  )









For the grey majority, the error bar swallows the estimate. Some MOEs are more than a hundred times the estimated change itself (Tract 306: −0.03 ± 8.3 points).
Next, the reliability table: the 15 largest statistically detectable increases, with each period’s CV colored by the Jurjevich thresholds. This is exactly the population of tracts an article like this one quotes from.

  arrange(desc(change)) %>%

    rate_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    rate_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate the claims
Supported. The citywide level checks out: my average tract rate for 2013–2017 is 26.1 percent against the article’s “26 percent,” up from 25.5 in 2006–2010. The direction is right too: among tracts with detectable change, increases (36) outnumber decreases (27), and the median change is +1.2 points. And concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty is real — 22 tracts exceed 55 percent, several in the mid-60s.
Not supported. The “startling surge” framing overstates what five-year tract data can show: 313 of 376 tracts (83 percent) are statistically indistinguishable from no change at all. Apparent jumps from very low baselines — exactly the Holmesburg (2%) and Mayfair (1%) pattern — are the least trustworthy numbers in the ACS: 44 tracts had unreliable 2006–2010 estimates (CV > 40), and a poverty rate of 1–2 percent typically carries an error band several times its size. Quoting “1 to 14 percent” without a margin of error is quoting endpoints of a noisy interval.
Cannot be determined. Every named-neighborhood figure — Fairhill 61%, Eastwick 12→26%, Holmesburg 2→19%, Mayfair 1→14% — would require the article’s tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, which it never published. The “22 majority-white neighborhoods” claim additionally needs poverty by race and a definition of majority-white. The white-poverty jump (14.8 → 19.4 percent) comes from a one-year survey, a different data product than the five-year comparison. The median-income claims rest on other tables I did not test.

section: Part 1: Rebuild the table you already know
text:
Part 1: Rebuild the table you already know
This is last week’s pull with a few more variables. Every line should look familiar.

philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    med_rent   = "B25064_001",   # median gross rent (our Y)
    med_inc    = "B19013_001",   # median household income
    total_pop  = "B01003_001",
    occ_units  = "B25003_001",   # occupied housing units
    renter_occ = "B25003_003",   # renter-occupied units
    edu_total  = "B15003_001",   # population 25+
    ba         = "B15003_022",
    ma         = "B15003_023",
    prof       = "B15003_024",
    phd        = "B15003_025"
  ),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)          # Pennsylvania South State Plane, feet

Now build the variables. A data frame goes in, a data frame comes out.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    pct_renter = renter_occE / occ_unitsE * 100,
    pct_ba     = (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / total_popE * 100,
    rent_se    = med_rentM / 1.645,
    rent_cv    = rent_se / med_rentE * 100
  )

Bring back the stations and count how many sit within half a mile of each tract. This is Week 4 with one new function.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(philly_tracts))

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_is_within_distance(., stations, dist = 0.5)))

Stop and look: st_is_within_distance() returns a list, one element per tract, holding the stations within range. What does lengths() do to that list?

your answer:
Returns a plain numeric vector with the length of each element.


Which tracts can we model?
A regression can’t use a row with a missing Y or X. R will quietly drop those rows, and later your residuals won’t line up with your tracts. So drop them yourself, on purpose, and count.

nrow(philly_tracts)

[1] 408

tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0,
         !is.na(med_rentE),
         !is.na(med_incE),
         !is.na(pct_ba),
         !is.na(pct_renter))

nrow(tracts)

[1] 377


Rule from Week 4, again: how many tracts did you lose? Which kind of tract has no median rent? (Hint: think about who lives there.)

The Week 3 habit comes first: plot the relationship before you fit anything.

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_incE, y = med_rentE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +

Stop and look: Does a straight line describe this cloud well everywhere, or does it bend? Where are the points that sit far from the line?

Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Week 5: Intro into machine learning
text:
Key Concepts
This lab was an introduction to machine learning for prediction, using linear regression. The core distinction is prediction (ŷ) versus inference (β̂): prediction asks “what will Y be for a new row,” while inference asks “does X cause Y and by how much.” The same coefficient gets read two different ways depending on the task. For grading a prediction model we use out-of-sample error: split the data into train and test sets, or better, use k-fold cross-validation, and report RMSE — the typical miss in dollars on unseen data. In-sample R² always improves when variables are added, so it cannot judge whether new variables truly help; CV RMSE can get worse, which makes it the honest grade. I also learned that our Y itself is noisy: ACS rent estimates carry margins of error, and a large residual in a high-CV tract may be survey fog rather than signal. Finally, mapping residuals showed that errors are not random in space — they cluster — which means the model is missing real spatial structure.

title: Week 5: Intro into machine learning
text:
Reflection
This lab changed how I read regression output. Before, I thought a significant p-value meant a variable was “good.” Now I see the p-value answers the inference question, while prediction is graded by CV RMSE on data the model has never seen — and a variable can fail the first test but pass the second. Plotting the residuals on a map was the most surprising part: the red clusters made it obvious that the model doesn’t know something about University City and the Northeast, and no table of coefficients shows that as clearly. The hardest part is letting go of causal language: it feels natural to say “stations raise rents,” but for this task all that matters is whether the variable helps the guess.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE

    # build your outcome, e.g. a percentage:

    # for a median or count, use the E and M columns directly.
    y_moe = tidycensus::moe_prop(

      denom = vehicle_hhE,
      moe_num = no_vehicleM,
      moe_denom = vehicle_hhM

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary_2023)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.446  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

nearest_station_idx <- st_nearest_feature(
  tract_pts,
  septa_stations
)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary_2023)),
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    
    dist_septa_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(
        tract_pts,
        septa_stations[nearest_station_idx, ],
        by_element = TRUE
      )
    ) / 5280
  )

f2 <- y ~ median_incomeE + poverty_pct + renter_pct + n_burglary
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m2", 
    added = "Residential Burglary count",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
    notes = "Raw count"
  )

# model 3

m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m3", 
    added = "Residential Burglary density",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
    notes = "Burglaries per square mile"
  )

# model 4

m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m4", 
    added = "Distance to 2023 SEPTA station",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
    notes = "Miles"
  )

Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Your answer: Residential burglary density helped the most among the initial spatial features, reducing CV RMSE from approximately 11.94 to 11.22 percentage points. Distance to the nearest 2023 SEPTA station also helped, reducing RMSE to approximately 11.43. The raw burglary count was the most disappointing because it only reduced RMSE to approximately 11.73; raw counts partly measure tract size rather than the intensity of neighborhood conditions.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: The baseline model used median household income, poverty rate, and renter share to predict the percentage of households without a vehicle. Its cross-validated RMSE was approximately 11.94 percentage points. Among the spatial features, residential burglary density helped the most, reducing RMSE to approximately 11.22. I do not interpret burglary as causing households to live without vehicles. Instead, its density may capture urban intensity and neighborhood conditions not fully represented by the ACS predictors. The raw burglary count was the most disappointing feature, reducing RMSE only to approximately 11.73. Raw counts are affected by tract size, whereas density is more comparable across tracts. Combining the useful spatial features with a curved income relationship produced the best model, with an RMSE of approximately 10.74. In the final model, the coefficient for renter share was approximately 0.294. The beta interpretation is that, holding poverty, income, burglary density, and distance to a SEPTA station constant, a one-percentage-point increase in renter share is associated with a 0.294-percentage-point increase in the predicted share of households without a vehicle. The y-hat interpretation is that two otherwise similar tracts differing by ten percentage points in renter share are predicted to differ by approximately 2.94 percentage points in their no-vehicle household shares. The final residual map shows smaller errors in many areas, but a cluster of underprediction remains around central Philadelphia. A useful next feature would be transit service frequency and job accessibility. Distance to a station does not measure how often service arrives or which destinations can be reached. Historical 2023 SEPTA GTFS schedules could provide these measures. Finally, the relationship between outcome CV and absolute final residual was nearly flat, with a correlation of approximately −0.05. This suggests that ACS sampling uncertainty explains little of the remaining error overall. Some residuals may contain statistical noise, but the remaining spatial pattern is more consistent with omitted transportation, land-use, and neighborhood characteristics.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Key Concepts
This lab was about making the linear model more flexible, one feature at a time, and letting cross-validated RMSE judge each addition. Logs handle skew: logging a predictor means a 1% change in income goes with about β/100 dollars more rent, while logging the outcome too turns the coefficient into an elasticity (a β% change), and predictions must be exp()’d back to dollars before computing RMSE. Squared terms let the relationship bend, but the turning point has to sit inside the data range — otherwise the curve is just bending, not turning. Categorical predictors enter as dummies against a reference level, and relevel() lets me pick a more natural baseline such as the largest group. Interactions go further: a plain categorical only shifts the line (base), while an interaction lets it tilt (delta), so a group’s slope is the sum of two coefficients. The same cv_rmse() from Part 0 grades every version, with log_outcome = TRUE whenever the outcome was logged, and fixed effects extend this dummy-variable idea to many groups at once.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Reflection
What stuck with me is how much the interpretation depends on where the log goes: β/100 dollars per 1% with only the predictor logged, an elasticity when both sides are logged, and dollars again only after exp() — the same model read three different ways. Reading an interaction as base + delta also made the coefficient table less intimidating, because the slope for the Outer ring is not one number but the sum of two. The turning-point check is a good guard against over-reading a squared term whose vertex sits far outside the sample. The hardest habit is restraint: a square, a factor, or an interaction each cost one line of code, but only CV RMSE decides whether they stay.

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary_2023)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.446  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.

  mutate(

    n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary_2023)),
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    
    dist_septa_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(
        tract_pts,
        septa_stations[nearest_station_idx, ],
        by_element = TRUE
      )
    ) / 5280

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m2", 
    added = "Residential Burglary count",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
    notes = "Raw count"
  )

  add_row(

    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
    notes = "Burglaries per square mile"

  add_row(

    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),

Your answer: Residential burglary density helped the most among the initial spatial features, reducing CV RMSE from approximately 11.94 to 11.22 percentage points. title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:

-27.721  -8.549  -0.983   7.699  43.547

I(dist_ch_mi^2)  0.09331    0.04854   1.922   0.0553 .

Multiple R-squared:  0.3792,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3759 
F-statistic: 115.4 on 2 and 378 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)

1  Core  79
2 Inner 134
3 Outer 168

summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-33.724 -10.328  -1.487   8.377  42.965 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   38.461      1.521  25.289   <2e-16 ***
ringInner     -3.650      1.917  -1.904   0.0577 .  
ringOuter    -20.512      1.844 -11.123   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 13.52 on 378 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3154,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3118 
F-statistic: 87.09 on 2 and 378 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: The baseline model used median household income, poverty rate, and renter share to predict the percentage of households without a vehicle. Its cross-validated RMSE was approximately 11.94 percentage points. Among the spatial features, residential burglary density helped the most, reducing RMSE to approximately 11.22. I do not interpret burglary as causing households to live without vehicles. Instead, its density may capture urban intensity and neighborhood conditions not fully represented by the ACS predictors. The raw burglary count was the most disappointing feature, reducing RMSE only to approximately 11.73. Raw counts are affected by tract size, whereas density is more comparable across tracts. Combining the useful spatial features with a curved income relationship produced the best model, with an RMSE of approximately 10.74.
In the final model, the coefficient for renter share was approximately 0.294. The beta interpretation is that, holding poverty, income, burglary density, and distance to a SEPTA station constant, a one-percentage-point increase in renter share is associated with a 0.294-percentage-point increase in the predicted share of households without a vehicle. The y-hat interpretation is that two otherwise similar tracts differing by ten percentage points in renter share are predicted to differ by approximately 2.94 percentage points in their no-vehicle household shares.
The final residual map shows smaller errors in many areas, but a cluster of underprediction remains around central Philadelphia. A useful next feature would be transit service frequency and job accessibility. Distance to a station does not measure how often service arrives or which destinations can be reached. Historical 2023 SEPTA GTFS schedules could provide these measures.
Finally, the relationship between outcome CV and absolute final residual was nearly flat, with a correlation of approximately −0.05. This suggests that ACS sampling uncertainty explains little of the remaining error overall. Some residuals may contain statistical noise, but the remaining spatial pattern is more consistent with omitted transportation, land-use, and neighborhood characteristics.
